thread.title: Loudoun, Fairfax officials talk Amazon, but won't bet the farm on HQ2

author: Daniel J. Sernovitz
title: Loudoun, Fairfax officials talk Amazon, but won't bet the farm on HQ2
text: – Staff Reporter, Washington Business Journal Sep 25, 2018, 2:57pm EDT Folks in Greater Washington have gotten pretty good at talking around t he region's chances of landing HQ2 . Whether due to superstition, fear of driving Amazon .com Inc. (NASDAQ: AMZN) away by saying too much, or just not wanting history to prove them wrong, few are willing to go so far as to say the region is a lock to win the biggest economic development prize in North America. Instead, it's about creating Amazon-friendly conditions. The notion was on full display Monday, when the Dulles Regional Chamber of Commerce held the latest in its series of Metro Monday events. Development activity around the Silver Line's Innovation Center station, adjacent to one of the region's prospective HQ2 locations , was technically the focus of this most recent installment, held at the Hyatt Regency Dulles. But Buddy Rizer , Loudoun County's economic development chief, said to fixate too much on any one company, whether it's Amazon or even Apple Inc . (NASDAQ: AAPL) with its big space search , would be to take too myopic a view. "The reason why you don’t ever hear me talking about Amazon or Apple, or read quotes about me talking about Amazon or Apple or anything like that, is because I really believe that that misses the picture," Rizer told the audience of about 80 people. "That misses the story that we’re trying to tell. What we’re talking about here is a special site that is going to be something extremely important to the future of our region." Rizer said Fairfax and Loudoun counties are focused on creating the kinds of conditions that will attract companies like Amazon and Apple, laying the groundwork for the region to become a major East Coast hub for technology companies, and the Silver Line's extension into Loudoun County is a big part of it. Those efforts, he said, have already yielded companies like Audi, Airbus, and, most recently, Microsoft Corp. "They want to create an environment where their workers want to come," Rizer said. "The future of these companies is not going to be where they build their buildings. The future of these companies is going to be where their future workforce wants to be, and by creating the right kind of environment, we know that they’re going to want to be at places like this." Locations in Northern Virginia, D.C. and suburban Maryland each made the short list for HQ2, an 8 million-square-foot prospect that could bring 50,000 jobs and a potential economic impact of around $5 billion in time. Sharon Bulova, chair of the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors, said Greater Washington's prominence among the 20 short-listed locations is a testament to the region's willingness to come together over a common goal. The Fairfax-Loudoun site includes the state-owned Center for Innovative Technology and private development sites The Hub and Waterside , which Amazon has toured as part of its HQ2 search. Those sites are poised for growth, regardless of where HQ2 goes. "Amazon would not even have paid attention, I don’t think, to this area except for the fact that we are extending the Metrorail line and that we have so much to offer," Bulova said. "But it’s not just about Amazon, and if Amazon never happens, and if Apple goes someplace else, what we've learned through this experience is how to work together more effectively and how to build assets and how to build opportunity here in this part of Fairfax County and Loudoun County." Tristan Simon, who is part of the team developing The Hub , said he is focused on creating the sort of environment that will help companies attract and retain tech talent. The Hub, formerly known as Dulles World Center, has been on the book in Loudoun for nearly a decade, but without any development taking place. It is planned for around 3.5 million square feet of office, along with nearly 1,300 residential units, 350 hotel rooms, a live music venue, retail, food emporium, open space and a commercial-scale hydroponic farm. "The partnership that we’ve felt here has been very exciting, and we’ve been to the bunker fighting very hard to hopefully bring this opportunity alive for the entire region," added Mark Masinter, also part of The Hub's development team. – Staff Reporter, Washington Business Journal Sep 25, 2018, 2:57pm EDT Related Content
